historical_timeline.summary: Febrile illness at 19 months; deaf and blind afterward.
Began learning language spelled into her hand.
Graduated cum laude from Radcliffe College.
Began her life's work for the American Foundation for the Blind.
Moved to Arcan Ridge, Easton, Connecticut.
Began eleven years of world tours to 35 countries.
Stroke; retired from public appearances and work (dated 1960 by one source).
Died in her sleep at Arcan Ridge.

claims.statement: Helen Keller was born on June 27, 1880, in Tuscumbia, Alabama.

In February 1882, at 19 months, she had a febrile illness that her doctor, as she later wrote, called acute congestion of the stomach and brain and thought she would not survive; the fever left suddenly, but she never saw or heard again.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her deafblindness from this illness is documented; the contemporary label does not identify a modern cause.

claims.statement: The cause of the 1882 illness is unknown; scarlet fever, meningitis, and rubella have been proposed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective suggestions without any record that could confirm them. Not used as a diagnosis.

source_links.locator: An unknown illness, perhaps rubella or scarlet fever

claims.statement: From March 1887 her teacher, a graduate of the Perkins School for the Blind, taught her language by spelling words into her hand; she learned the manual alphabet and raised print for blind readers, and began to learn speech at 10.

In her own account, others spoke to her by spelling into her hand with the single-hand manual alphabet while she rested her hand lightly on theirs; she spoke for herself, read the lips of some people by touch, and read and wrote braille.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents her own communication methods, which the synthetic care plan follows.

claims.statement: In 1904 she graduated cum laude from Radcliffe College, the first deafblind person to earn a college degree.

From 1924 she worked as a public spokesperson for the American Foundation for the Blind for the rest of her life, and from 1946 she made world tours to 35 countries in 11 years on behalf of people with disabilities.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents her working life and travel into her late seventies.

claims.statement: A receipt dated September 1911 records the purchase of an artificial eye for her.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The receipt does not say which eye or whether an eye was removed; the AFB notes that early photographs show an oddly shaped left eye.

claims.statement: She lived at Arcan Ridge in Easton, Connecticut, from the late 1930s for the rest of her life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Perkins gives 1939 for the move; Connecticut History gives 1936.

claims.statement: Her father died in 1896 and her mother in 1921.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Causes of death are not recorded in the cited source.

claims.statement: She had a stroke and retired from public appearances and work; Perkins dates this to 1961 and the American Foundation for the Blind to 1960.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The stroke is documented; its type is not recorded, and the year differs between sources. Both dates fall after the true-frame index date, so it appears only in the timeline.

claims.statement: She died in her sleep at Arcan Ridge on June 1, 1968, a few weeks before her 88th birthday.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Provide disability-competent primary and preventive care to a 78-year-old writer and advocate who has been deafblind since infancy: communicate with her directly through a qualified tactile interpreter and braille materials on her terms, with the time that takes; evaluate a fall by CDC STEADI and prevent the next one with strength and balance exercise and home changes; screen bone density; adapt cognitive and mood screening honestly; protect the sense of touch she relies on; and give the same screening and prevention any woman her age would get.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Keller returns two weeks after her first visit, through the same qualified tactile interpreter, and saw the geriatric medicine consultant this morning. She has had no further falls. She has stopped using the back steps until the handrail is extended and walks outdoors only with her sighted guide. Her bone density scan was done this morning. She had no dizziness, palpitations, or loss of consciousness before the March fall; she says she reached for a rail that was not there and missed the last step. She takes no regular medicines and no over-the-counter sleep aids. She wears lace-up walking shoes. She asks for her results and the plan in braille.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Keller returns for her six-month review through a qualified tactile interpreter. She has had no falls. The occupational therapist visited in July: handrails are now on both sides of every step, tactile edge strips are on the steps, her smoke and carbon monoxide alarms now shake her bed, and she wears an alert button. She finished physical therapy in June and exercises daily. Her August cystitis cleared within three days on nitrofurantoin; during those nights she used the bedside rail and did not fall. She has made a second speaking trip. She notices no change in the feeling in her fingers.

documentation.chief_complaint: Burning on passing urine and frequency for two days

hpi.narrative: Ms. Keller is a 79-year-old woman, deafblind since infancy, who called by text relay for a same-day visit. The history was taken through the clinic's on-call qualified tactile interpreter, who arrived 30 minutes after she did; she chose to wait rather than have her assistant interpret. For two days she has had burning on passing urine, frequency, and urgency, with no leakage. She has had no fever, chills, flank or back pain, nausea, vaginal discharge, or blood she could detect, and her assistant has noticed no change in her urine. She had one similar episode years ago that cleared with a short course of antibiotics. She has no allergies and takes no regular medicines. She is drinking well. She is due to travel to speak in ten days.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Keller returns for her subsequent annual wellness visit, her first at this clinic; her initial wellness visit was with her previous physician. The visit was conducted through a qualified tactile interpreter, with the room arranged so her hand could rest on the interpreter's and Dr. Strand seated within reach, so she could read speech by touch when she wished. Her August cystitis cleared within three days on nitrofurantoin. She has had no falls since the one that brought her here in March, and five weeks ago her chair stand and balance had improved to the age norms. She does her strength and balance exercises daily. She has made two speaking trips this year with a sighted guide. She has no new concerns. She wants her advance care plan updated with her communication passport.

referral.pertinent_history: Deafblind since an illness at 19 months. She receives language by tactile fingerspelling with the one-hand manual alphabet, speaks for herself, and reads braille; please speak to her directly through the interpreter and touch her hand to signal your presence. Three weeks ago she missed the last step where her back-step handrail ends; no injury and no dizziness or blackout. Timed Up and Go 13.5 seconds, 30-second chair stand 9, tandem stance 6 seconds. Orthostatic vital signs normal. No medicines. Hemoglobin, metabolic panel, vitamin D (31 ng/mL), and B12 (520 pg/mL) normal; PHQ-9 2 in braille. Bone density scan booked. She writes daily, travels to speak, and lives with a long-time assistant
questions: Is there any medical contributor to the fall beyond the hazard and reduced leg strength and balance?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Keller is seen at the request of Dr. Strand, through a qualified tactile interpreter, in a double-length appointment; she answered for herself throughout. She missed the last step where the back-step handrail ends three weeks ago and sat down hard without injury; she had no warning symptoms. She has had no other falls in the past year. She notices that rising from low chairs takes more effort than it did a few years ago. She has no urinary incontinence, no nocturia beyond once, no weight loss, and no change in the feeling in her fingers or feet, which she checks closely because she reads and receives language by touch. She sleeps seven hours, drinks a glass of wine with dinner a few times a week, and takes no medicines. She is independent in all activities of daily living; her assistant drives, shops, and reads her print mail

exam.finding: Alert, warm, and precise; speech clear with attention
Hip and knee strength 4+ of 5; rises from a standard chair with one push of the arms
Normal sensation and pulses; well-fitting lace-up shoes

assessment.display: Fall at home with increased fall risk
assessment.assessment: A mechanical fall at an environmental hazard, made more probable by reduced hip and knee strength and balance. There is no orthostatic hypotension, no medicine, no neuropathy, no cognitive impairment, and no continence or nutritional problem. Vision is not a modifiable factor here; she moves by touch, rails, and a sighted guide

Standard screening tools depend on vision or hearing, and none is validated for people who are deafblind. A tactile interview with fingerspelled word recall, spoken verbal fluency, and serial sevens, interpreted by a qualified tactile interpreter, shows no impairment. Use the same method each year so that any change is measured against her own baseline

Touch is her main channel for language and reading, and it is fully intact. Her greatest risks in illness are communication barriers: being examined without warning, consent taken without a qualified interpreter, or isolation in hospital
Low bone mass with FRAX risk below the treatment thresholds; medicine is not indicated

recommendations: Home physical therapy for progressive strength and balance training twice a week for 12 weeks, then a daily home program; a qualified tactile interpreter at the first sessions and whenever new exercises are taught

Occupational therapy home visit: handrails on both sides of every step to the bottom step, tactile edge strips, clear routes, vibrating smoke and carbon monoxide alarms with a bed shaker, and a wearable alert button
Repeat Timed Up and Go, chair stand, and balance tests after the exercise program
No vitamin D supplement for fall prevention, since her level is adequate; dietary calcium of about 1,200 mg a day
Repeat the tactile cognitive check yearly at the wellness visit by the same method
Write a hospital communication passport in braille and print with her, and record her health care agent and wishes; review them at her annual wellness visit
